fields.h1: Build an Enneagram Quiz That Finds a Center, Then a Type
fields.hero_description: Build an enneagram quiz that sorts answers by center and type, and saves every result to a table you own.
fields.features_heading: The Working Parts of an Enneagram Quiz
fields.features_subheading: One prompt builds the quiz, the nine result pages, and the table behind them. Ask for a change in plain words, and the build updates.
fields.feature_1:
Every option mapped to one type

Name the result set in your prompt: all nine types, or the three centers. Emergent writes scenario questions, maps each option to one result, and rewords any question you ask it to.
fields.feature_2:
A result page for each type

Each type gets its own result screen: a short description, what the lean means, and which wing to read next. Edit the wording by prompt until it sounds like you wrote it yourself.
fields.feature_3:
Answers saved to a table you own

Each finished quiz lands as a row in a database you own, with the type, the center, and every answer behind it. Filter rows by type before a session, or export the whole table.
fields.feature_4:
Email capture before the result

Ask for an email on the last screen, so the result is the reward. The address saves with the type it landed on, and the app can sync both to any mailing tool that has an API.
fields.feature_5:
Alerts the moment someone finishes

Get a Slack or email alert when a client or teammate finishes, with the type lean in the message. Reminders go to the people who started the quiz and stopped partway through it.
fields.feature_6:
Your quiz, your code

Run the quiz on your own site with no cap on how many people answer it. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and change any screen of it directly.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Enneagram Quizzes, Four Different Jobs
fields.tab_content_1:
A type lean lands before session 1

Larkwood Coaching sends every new client a 27-question intake quiz with the first session invite. Tessa Vale finishes on her phone, her answers lean Type 8 in the Body center, and her coach gets an email the moment she submits. Every answer sits in the client table, read before the call.
fields.tab_content_2:
18 answers in with a week to go

Calder Point Advisory booked a June offsite and asked all 21 consultants to take the quiz first. With a week to go, the count stands at 18 of 21: 8 lean Heart, 6 Head, and 4 Body. The facilitator reads the split on the dashboard, sends 3 reminders, and plans the breakout groups from the counts.
fields.tab_content_3:
Signups that arrive already tagged by type

Renata Voss gives readers a reason to subscribe: a 12-question enneagram quiz linked from her Tuesday newsletter. In May, 530 people finish it and 221 leave an email for the full result. Each address lands in her list tagged with its type, so the welcome email can speak to it.
fields.tab_content_4:
One rule sorts 54 people into 3 rooms

Stonebridge Church runs a quiz night to seed its new small groups. All 54 signups take the same short quiz, and a sorting rule does the rest: Body leans to Room 1, Heart to Room 2, Head to Room 3. The split lands at 17, 21, and 16, and every name is on a room list before coffee is poured.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Enneagram Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create an enneagram quiz that maps answers to the types you choose and tests the path to every result.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide what a finished quiz names: one type of nine, or a center for a shorter sort. Nine results need a longer question list and richer result pages; three centers keep a lunch-hour team session moving. Write the choice into your first prompt.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Paired statements and scenario options both work. The Enneagram Institute's RHETI runs 144 paired statements; keep a self-serve web quiz near 25. Pick one format and hold it: takers settle into a rhythm instead of relearning every screen.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask what someone does when a plan collapses, not whether they are a perfectionist. Write 3 options per question with one option for each center, matched in length and tone. An option that sounds flattering skews the whole map; Emergent rewords any that feel stiff.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Map each option to exactly one type or center, then decide what a tie does before anyone plays. A simple rule lets the first-listed result win. Put the mapping in your prompt, and the quiz scores itself the same way every time.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Open each result with how that lean shows up on a good week and on a bad one, then point to a next read. Frame every line as a lean, not a verdict: the result is where answers point today, not a fixed trait.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test the path to every result
fields.howto_step_6_des: Answer the quiz once per result, straight through, and confirm each one can come up. Check the tie rule with a split answer set, and read the table row each run writes. A result no path reaches is a question map error.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Share one link in the session invite, the newsletter, or the group chat, and watch the table fill. Counts by type tell you if one option set skews the sort; reword it by prompt and the next taker gets the fix.
fields.hero_prompt: Build an enneagram quiz for my coaching intake that names each client's likely type and saves their answers to my client table.

faq_plan.a: An enneagram quiz is a short set of questions that maps your answers to one of the Enneagram's nine basic personality types. Shorter versions sort answers into a center first: there are three centers, with three types in each. The quiz on this page plays that center step.

faq_plan.q: How do I create an enneagram quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe it in one prompt to Emergent's AI survey builder: the results you want, how many questions, and what happens when someone finishes. Emergent builds the quiz, the result screens, and the table that stores every answer, and you change any of it by prompting.

faq_plan.q: Can I keep an enneagram quiz free for everyone who takes it?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Keep the enneagram quiz free for takers and still request an address before the full result. Emergent is free to start, and the free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: How many results can an enneagram personality quiz support?
faq_plan.a: Nine, one per type, when the quiz runs about 25 questions; at 9 to 12 questions, aim for a center instead. Each result needs several questions that can point to it, or one stray answer decides it. A hair type quiz picks from far fewer results, and 8 questions can carry it.

faq_plan.q: What should an enneagram type quiz show on the result screen?
faq_plan.a: Show the type, a paragraph on how that lean looks in daily life, and its wings. A wing is one of the two types adjacent to the taker's type on the circle. End with one next step, such as a longer test or a coaching call.

faq_plan.q: How should an enneagram types quiz handle a tie between two types?
faq_plan.a: Ask one tiebreaker question. When two types finish level, show a final question whose options point only to those two. That lets the taker settle it, which is fairer than letting the order of your result list decide.

faq_plan.q: Should a short enneagram quiz sort by center before type?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if it has fewer than about 15 questions. The Body center holds Types 8, 9, and 1; Heart holds 2, 3, and 4; Head holds 5, 6, and 7. A center is a result a short quiz can support. A general personality quiz has no such grouping to lean on.

faq_plan.q: How do I phrase enneagram quiz results so they do not read as a label?
faq_plan.a: Write each result as a lean, such as your answers lean toward Type 4, never as a fixed verdict. A free enneagram quiz describes preferences. Say that in one line on the result screen, and point takers to a longer test for more depth.

faq_plan.q: Should an enneagram quiz show scores for all nine types?
faq_plan.a: Yes, below the main result. Lead with the top type, then list all nine scores in order. A taker whose top two types are close can then read about both. Ask for the breakdown in your prompt, and Emergent builds it as a chart on the result screen.

faq_plan.q: Can one app run an enneagram quiz alongside other quizzes?
faq_plan.a: Yes, in an app Emergent builds: one app can hold an enneagram quiz for self-awareness and a career quiz for role interests, keyed to the same email address. Emergent builds both from prompts. Data lives in a database the user owns, with both sets of answers side by side.

quiz.title: Which Enneagram Center Do You Lead With?
quiz.intro: Nine everyday scenarios, three answers each. Your result names the center your answers lean toward, Body, Heart, or Head, and the three types that sit in it.

questions.text: A plan with friends falls apart an hour before it starts. What is your first move?

options.text: Pick a new plan and tell everyone where to meet
Check that nobody feels let down by the change
Look up what else is open before saying anything

questions.text: Your team gets a vague new project. What do you want first?

options.text: Some research and a clear picture of the risks
A start date and the first task to get moving
A sense of who is on it and how they feel about it

questions.text: A friend asks for honest feedback on their new business idea. You start with:

options.text: What they hope it will mean for them
The questions they have not answered yet
Whether it feels right in your gut

questions.text: Which compliment would mean the most to you?

options.text: You always know what to do next
You think things through like nobody else
You make people feel seen

questions.text: You have a free evening with no plans. What sounds best?

options.text: Dinner with someone you have not seen in a while
A walk, a workout, or a project with your hands
A long read or a documentary on a new topic

questions.text: A decision at work goes against you. What lingers longest?

options.text: Going over the reasoning to find the flaw
Wondering how it makes you look to others
A hot sense that it simply was not fair

questions.text: In a group discussion, you are most likely to:

options.text: Say plainly what you think should happen
Notice who has not spoken and draw them in
Listen, then ask the question nobody asked

questions.text: When you picture a good week, what makes it good?

options.text: Real progress you can point to by Friday
Time that left you closer to the people around you
Something new that finally made sense to you

questions.text: Before a big trip, which part do you enjoy most?

options.text: Reading up on the place and making a plan
Imagining the moments you will share with others
Packing, booking, and getting out the door

results.title: You Lead With the Body Center
results.description: Your answers lean toward acting on instinct: you size up a situation fast and move. The Body center holds Types 8, 9, and 1. Read those three and see which one sounds most like your week.

results.title: You Lead With the Heart Center
results.description: Your answers lean toward reading people: you notice how a moment lands for others before you act. The Heart center holds Types 2, 3, and 4. Read those three and see which one sounds most like your week.

results.title: You Lead With the Head Center
results.description: Your answers lean toward thinking it through: you gather what you need to know before you commit. The Head center holds Types 5, 6, and 7. Read those three and see which one sounds most like your week.

plan.angle: The top 10 is all take-the-test sites (Truity, Enneagram Institute, dedicated test pages), zero builder slots. This page serves both intents the way the fitness page does: a short playable enneagram quiz on the page (9 questions that name the center your answers lean toward), then the builder story the SERP ignores: coaches, facilitators, newsletter writers, and small-group leaders who want their own quiz, with every answer in a table they own. The expert hook is structure: a good enneagram quiz narrows by center first (Body, Heart, Head), then type, so the page teaches the two-stage design none of the test sites explain.
